turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I shall not debate the matter with you, Sandip. I have already taken measures to ensure the safety of my tenantry, and I will not tolerate any further harassment of them.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Sandip, perhaps we should hear Nikhil out before we dismiss his concerns.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Bimala, you are always so eager to hear Nikhil out, I suppose it's because you're more afraid of the Mussulmans than I am. Your gentle soul must be trembling with fear, isn't it, Bimala?

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Sandip, I think you're misunderstanding Nikhil's concerns. It's not about being afraid, but about taking responsibility for our people's safety.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Nikhil, you're as serious as a wet hen. Can't you see I'm enjoying the sunshine while you're worried about the shadows?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I will not be swayed by your levity, Sandip. The situation is grave, and I will not stand idly by while your carelessness puts my tenantry at risk.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Ah, Nikhil, you're as serious as a wet hen, and I'm as concerned as I am about the price of silk fabrics at the next fair. I'll take your warnings to heart, but only after I've finished this poem I'm writing.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I will not be mocked, Sandip. The safety of my people is not a subject for jest.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Oh, Nikhil, do pardon me if I'm not as solemn as you, but I'm sure the tenantry can take care of themselves. After all, they're not as delicate as my wife's feelings, are they?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your levity is a poor shield, Sandip, and I will not rest until my people are secure.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Oh, come now, Nikhil, do spare me the dramatics. I'm sure your tenantry is as safe as my garden is from your attempts at poetry.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Sandip, perhaps Nikhil's warnings should be given more consideration, don't you think?

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: I'm not afraid of your Mussulman friends, Nikhil, and neither should you be. Why, I'm sure they'd rather listen to my poetry than your prosaic warnings.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Sandip, perhaps we could discuss the specifics of Nikhil's warnings, and how we might address them together?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your levity is a liability, Sandip, and I will not be swayed by your jests.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: I assure you, Nikhil, my poetry is far more effective at warding off attacks than your dull sermons on loyalty and duty.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I will not engage in frivolous conversation, Sandip. The threat to your safety is real, and I will not be ignored.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Fancy that, Nikhil, you think a few whispered threats from the Mussulmans can rattle me? I'm a zamindar, after all!

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: I will not stand idly by while you trivialize the situation, Sandip. Your fate, and that of your family, depends on your willingness to take this threat seriously.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: What's the plan, Nikhil? Are you going to rally the troops and put up a fight, or merely cower behind your warnings?

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I say, Nikhil, don't you keep Browning among your books here? I was just telling Queen Bee of our college club. Do you remember that contest of ours over the translation of those lines from Browning? You don't?

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I managed to get together the words to render it into Bengali, somehow, but the result was hardly likely to be a 'joy forever' to the people of Bengal. I really did think at one time that I was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence was kind enough to save me from that disaster. Do you remember old Dakshina? If he had not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet. I remember his rendering to this day ...

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: No, Queen Bee, it is no use rummaging those bookshelves. Nikhil has ceased to read poetry since his marriage--perhaps he has no further need for it. But I suppose 'the fever fit of poesy', as the Sanskrit has it, is about to attack me again.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I have come to give you a warning, Sandip

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: About the fever fit of poesy?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: For some time, Mahomedan preachers have been about stirring up the local Mussulmans. They are all wild with you, and may attack you any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Are you come to advise flight?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I have come to give you information, not to offer advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Had these estates been mine, such a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for me. If, instead of trying to frighten me, you give them a taste of your intimidation, that would be worthier both of you and me. Do you know that your weakness is weakening your neighbouring zamindars also?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I did not offer you my advice, Sandip. I wish you, too, would refrain from giving me yours. Besides, it is useless. And there is another thing I want to tell you. You and your followers have been secretly worrying and oppressing my tenantry. I cannot allow that any longer. So I must ask you to leave my territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: For fear of the Mussulmans, or is there any other fear you have to threaten me with?
